title: Anchoring

scenes.text: A *random number* can change your answer
scenes.vo: A totally random number can change what you think. Even when you know it's random.

scenes.text: Scientists spun a wheel that stopped on *10* or *65*
scenes.vo: Scientists spun a wheel in front of people. It stopped on either 10 or 65.

scenes.text: Then asked: what % of countries in a list are *African*?
scenes.vo: Then they asked everyone the same quiz question, about how many countries in a big list were from Africa.
People who saw 10 guessed low. People who saw 65 guessed much higher. The wheel had nothing to do with the question!
This is called anchoring. The first number you see becomes an anchor, and your brain doesn't drift far from it.
It's why online shops show a crossed-out price. You see 2,999 first, so 999 feels super cheap, even if that's the normal price.

scenes.text: Before you look at the price, decide what it's *worth to you*
scenes.vo: So before you look at the price, decide what something is actually worth to you.

caption:
The first number you see quietly controls every number after it. ⚓ That's anchoring, and shops use it on you every day.

Have you ever fallen for a 'was ₹2,999' price? 👇
source: Tversky, A. & Kahneman, D. (1974). Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases. Science, 185(4157).
